It is assumed that the radiological device acts as a volumetric and asymmetrically shielded radiation source, and the mobile platform (with SDF capabilities) would navigate to it and autonomously perform passive radiological measurements to characterize the R/N device. These measurements are presently performed by hand and used to guide future actions. The measurements need also be correlated with radiographic and any other active imaging modalities used to characterize the source. Such correlation could be accomplished by post-hoc alignment, or the active characterization system could be integrated into the autonomous platform. Being able to report on dose-rates in the vicinity of the device is critical for the manual render-safe operation. Being able to compute a dose-rate map in the vicinity of the device, so that one could chart a safe (human) path to the device, is another enhancement that would be useful. Being able to couple an internal activity distribution with radiography would be the most impactful but hardest to achieve capability. 4.3 Contamination Characterization and Mapping Contamination characterization and mapping consists of establishing the spatial bounds of a radiation-contaminated area, e.g., that might occur after the explosion of a radiological device; determining activities/concentrations of contamination and contamination species; and supporting determinations that areas have been decontaminated. Unlike the stabilization and render-safe application, multiple distributions of different radiation sources are possible. However, the application of SDF is the same - approximate scene-setting, dimensions and bounds of the contaminated area, constructing dose maps, and supporting autonomous systems. The standard contamination mapping use-case is similar to the one in Sec. 4.2 in the sense that it requires one to map out a radiative environment (though the source is typically much larger in spatial extent), and consequently the required enhancements are much the same. However, since one would be required to reconstruct a dose-map caused by a wide distribution of radioactivity, the emphasis would be less on characterizing the contents of a package and more on quickly characterizing a broad contaminated area.
